title: Speed limits on biomolecular processes from fundamental physical constants
abstract: Many of the timescales of life have speed limits set by quantum-mechanical constraints along with non-fundamental quantities, such as the temperature of the environment, which are however bounded by anthropic considerations. Here, some of such speed limits are examined, including those for the rates of elementary chemical reactions and biomolecular folding. Limitations of simple back-of-envelope estimates are also discussed.
summary: This paper investigates the theoretical speed limits governing life processes, such as chemical reactions and protein folding. It uses advanced statistical mechanical tools like Kramers' theory to relate these rates to fundamental physical constants. The work highlights how anthropic arguments constrain molecular dynamics by linking kinetic timescales to universal ratios.
main_problem: The paper examines fundamental physical constraints that set speed limits on various biomolecular processes, such as chemical reaction rates and protein folding kinetics.
main_result: It establishes relationships between characteristic timescales (e.g., diffusion time vs. kinetic time) governed by the Arrhenius ratio, suggesting deep connections between molecular dynamics and fundamental constants.
method: The analysis combines classical statistical mechanics tools like the Langevin equation and Kramers' theory with quantum-mechanical rate estimates derived from transition state theory.
model_or_system: The models include elementary chemical reactions in solution (governed by Arrhenius law) and protein folding/diffusion, which is treated as a random coil undergoing Brownian motion in conformational space.

Reaction rates ($

important_parameters: Fundamental constants like $\hbar, k_B$, temperature $T$, molecular dimensions ($R, a$), and friction coefficients ($\gamma$).
main_assumptions: Key approximations include using Stokes' formula for friction and assuming the validity of Kramers theory across different damping regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first analyzing simple chemical reactions using Eyring/Kramers estimates, then extending this framework to macromolecular dynamics like protein folding, culminating in a discussion of how anthropic constraints tie these physical limits together.
why_interesting: It bridges concepts from open quantum systems (dissipation via Langevin equation) and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (rate theories), providing concrete examples where fundamental constants dictate biological feasibility.
